A short and breezy classical JRPG, with heavy emphasis on the "classic"- Ara Fell's dominant feel is that of professionalism- sometimes to its benefit, sometimes to its detriment. While it's indeed a solidly built game that's visually and mechanically polished, what lies within is played so safely, and built upon such well trodden ground that it's difficult to really find anything to say about it at all besides "it's enjoyable".

Chances are that if you've played one or two of the big name classics from the SNES era, or if you're familiar with the most stock tropes for story, characters, and mechanics, you've already played Ara Fell without knowing it. That's not to say that it's outright bad for any particular reason- what's here is more akin to "JRPG comfort food" that's going to tick all the boxes, but really doesn't take a bold enough step in any one direction to stand out or be deeply satisfying.

There are certainly some things here that are more unique- the setting comes with a nice package of in-universe explanation for geology, culture, food/water, and other such things on the floating islands, as well as a somewhat different approach to the in game economy, focusing more on exploration and resource gathering to craft items and upgrade gear rather than just purchasing it (though the option is still available).

But really, Ara Fell doesn't get a whole lot of use out of either, and for the most part its easy to forget that there's anything much different from a standard, linear progression and medieval-toned setting you'd find in any old game. The story feels rather disconnected from the nature of the setting outside of its broadest strokes- it's a stock plot that could happen anywhere, to almost any fantasy setting, which is kind of a waste of what could be a unique hook. Even though there's some depth to how it all works, it still ends up feeling more like set dressing.

Crafting wise, materials are gated in such a way that it mostly still feels like a linear progression of obtaining new gear- so while you have somewhat of a free range to explore, you can't really ever DO much with that free range- it feels a little tacked on, despite the fact that the loop of resource acquisition and exploration is satisfying in of itself. Not to mention that the game is easy enough that item crafting is almost an afterthought entirely- I think over the 15 hour runtime I used maybe 3 or 4 items, tops.

A big part of this is that unlike the majority of RPGs, HP and MP are refilled to max after every encounter in Ara Fell- in effect, one of the main points of differentiation in the game is also one of its greatest weaknesses, as it so deeply undercuts a large part of its gameplay loop. While its fun at first to be able to go all out in every encounter, and it helps the early game feel punchier, it eventually flattens everything out to constantly running the same optimal loops in combat.

In the end there's no real dynamism, strategy, or resource management outside of a handful of boss fights. You just kind of do the exact same thing in every fight, over and over, and every now and then get to upgrade a skill or a piece of gear along a (mostly) linear path. It feels strangely at odds with a crafting system that would otherwise provide some opportunity for tight resourcing- managing between your items, gear, and stats- and would have been engaging. But instead it's all sort of shaved off, played safe, not taking those risks that could've been rewarding.

Really, the narrative plays out in much the same way- it feels rather flat, linear, and expected. The characters are fairly weak, and kind of just play out some standard archetypal roles without much extra fanfare. All the seemingly "legally required" JRPG beats are in there- a throwaway romance, double and triple crossing baddies, a jailbreak subplot, the evil regent poisoning the king, characters holding the idiot ball so a boss/plot point can happen, etc. The main plot arc itself even revolves around the same "collect the macguffins to save the world" thing everyone's heard before.

So while there's certainly enough wiggle room in the setting and with the basic lore that something more interesting could have been done, once again, it's all played safe- go for the stock plot, stay on the path, look pretty, be polished. If you're at all familiar with the genre, you'll pretty much guess everything that happens well before it makes the expected move. If you're looking for the meat-and-potatoes RPG experience with some management and character building, or some challenging puzzles or fights, this really isn't it- but if you're looking for a unique story or memorable characters, or a world to dig into, this... also isn't it?

...Which kind of leaves it in a weird place for me- because it's still a fine game. It's visually appealing- probably the best use of the REFMAP tiles I've personally seen, along with nice custom assets. It's mechanically sound, even if it doesn't do anything particularly special. It's competently written, even if it's entirely stock under the surface. It's honestly still an impressive feat for a small team- it's just the kind of thing that feels so average that it hurts.

It's one of the few times I've finished a game and felt almost nothing about it besides "I wonder what I'm playing next?". It's something that I can't really say I'd recommend to people OR tell people to stay away from- for better or worse it's just "a game".  

(Since I have to pick yes or no on Steam, though, it errs on the side of "sure")

Ara Fell really brought back that nostalgic feeling I used to get playing FF dawn of souls on my Game Boy Advance SP as a kid. It doesn’t fully reach that same level, but it absolutely captures that classic jrpg/rpg charm in a way that’s hard to find now.

I found myself thinking about the game throughout the day at work, planning my next moves, and even staying up later than I should just to push the story forward, grind a bit, or take on side bosses. That kind of pull is rare for me, and it says a lot about how engaging the game is. I’ve tried games like Octopath Traveler, but they just feel bland in comparison. Ara Fell made me genuinely happy while playing and really took me to another place.

Nothing here felt “new” in terms of mechanics, but somehow it still felt refreshing. It just does what it does really well. Do I wish there was more? Absolutely!!! But honestly, the best games always leave me wanting more, never wanting the story to end, even though you know it has to.

Overall, I’m 110% happy with my purchase. If you’re into story-driven jrpg/rpg’s, character progression, boss fights, and exploration, this is definitely worth picking up.

Honestly, it was way more entertaining than loading up another FPS shooter XD

Ara Fell is a simple JRPG with a straightforward, charming story. Its combat is not complex, even on the hardest difficulty. You’ll rarely face a truly punishing encounter, and catching up in levels is always easy.

At first, I was hesitant to recommend it. The gameplay can feel repetitive. With a party of four (which you’ll gather quickly) and each character has a minimal set of skills, and gear is upgraded linearly, with enhancements that feel minor rather than game changing. The difficulty stays low, rarely demanding special tactics or posing a real threat, which was initially a letdown.

But then it clicked: that’s the entire point. Why? Because this is the perfect game for someone new to the genre: a gentle introduction to the pacing of a JRPG.

The story is short, but written with clear passion. It has a certain charm, like revisiting a beloved childhood tale where you become the hero, told in a way that feels inspiring rather than childish. 

The world of Ara Fell is an inviting place, and even the brief narrative fleshes it out enough to make you curious about its history and future. I only wish there were more of it to see.
In the end, the blend of simple mechanics, approachable difficulty, and a nostalgic story turns Ara Fell from an average RPG into a genuinely pleasant experience for anyone wanting to wade into the genre’s vast waters.

I’d fully recommend it to someone chasing that childhood-story feeling, or to a newcomer looking for an easier start. I would not, however, recommend it to experienced players seeking deep systems, complex combat, or a serious challenge.

TLDR:

Ara Fell is a charming, heartfelt JRPG that serves as an excellent first adventure for the genre, but likely too simple for veterans looking for complexity or difficulty.

What a charming little game. If this had come out on the SNES or the PS1 it would be regarded as a classic.

I bought this ages ago and put it aside when the controller I was using didn't register inputs. I tested my dual shock 4 with it recently and it worked. I enable Steam input for all my games and I don't know if that made a difference, but either way I had zero issues completing it.

What immediately stood out to me was the strength of the dialog. The characters are written believably. There's a good mix of humor and seriousness; none of the humor is cringy Marvel-style quips that takes all the tension out of every scene. The story managed to hold my attention throughout and I genuinely liked all of the main party members (and several of the side characters) by the time I was finished.

The combat and leveling is fairly straightforward. If you're familiar with JRPGs there's nothing that's going to blow your mind here. What is here is competently done. It would be too thin to sustain a longer experience, but for a 10-15 hour playthrough, it does exactly what it needs to do. There's enough buffs and debuffs to reward different approaches and cater to specific playstyles. It's on the easier side once you get your characters powered up, but it's difficult to balance these kinds of games once you have the ability to become overpowered so I don't consider that a negative. I could have spent less time leveling up and nobody forced me to upgrade all my gear. I felt like I was rewarded for putting the effort in to beef up my party and make each member god-like in their own way. Considering that I'm comparing it to games like Final Fantasy VI by saying it would be a classic in that era - that's exactly how I played FFVI and the only exception is challenge runs.

This is very competently made with a lot of charm and beautiful pixel art. If you love old school games like Lunar or Lufia, this is well worth your time.

The only real complaint that I have is that some of the environments are ridiculously large and sometimes it is difficult to see items on the ground, where you can walk, or staircases that will take you to the next part of the area. On that last one - there was a point where I was stumped for about ten minutes until I realized there was a staircase behind a tree. In some other cases, ledges that looked to tall to jump up or down were actually able to be jumped and I only found that out when I got desperate enough to run up to the edges of the environment while hitting the jump button just to see if something would happen. These were small annoyances overall, but they did detract from my experience.

This is absolutely worth your time if you enjoy classic RPGs.

Okay look, this is a really impressive game... or it was when it came out.

First off, playing this game in the first place is kind of a pain. 

You have to ruin it in windowed mode or deal with screen tearing.

Then there is the gameplay. The Battle System works and that is the best I can say about it. It's the most standard battle system you could ever imagine. There is not a single interesting thing about it and the only time it is ever anything but tedious is in some boss fights (they are not fun either mind you, just not actively tedious). 

The character are not unlikeable but they are also nothing special and the story is pretty boring. 

The game has also incredibly tonal issues where it tried to combine light-hearted humor and darker tones but doesn't really nail it. 

Not to mention that it is very lacking in the gameplay department.

So yeah, this game is a wonderful representative of early indie games but is it a good game, sadly no.

Is it bad, no either.

It is aggressively average and I will be honest, an average game is in many ways worse than an outright bad game (if it is such in a janky or overreaching their ambitions way) because an average game is not just not fun, it is boring.

This game is committing the unforgivable sin of advertising itself as a cozy, leisurely turn-based game (even with a story mode and explicit support for color blind people, too!) and then out of the blue going back on this promise with a timed event that is impossible to complete for me and many others even in story mode. This severe debasement of the game was mendaciously added in the "enhanced" edition, which of course came out after a lot of the reviews and walkthroughs were written. Obviously it takes more than 2 hours to reach this point, so even if you bought the game directly on Steam you can't easily get it reimbursed.

The developers probably did this without thinking, but players complained about this already many years ago. All they are offering is to edit save files if you send them to them, as if it was somehow the fault of affected players that the game cheats in this way. Not acceptable. They didn't even fix it for story mode. Whether you play in expert mode (which isn't that hard) or in story mode or anything in between: You always get exactly 35 seconds for what seems impossible to achieve in less than 40 seconds. My reactions have always been too slow for action games, and my patience for any form of physical training is minimal. But it's not even that extreme in my case. A paraplegic person getting to this point with mouth controls or something obviously doesn't have a chance.

(PS: I am playing with a controller on Linux and tried first with the Linux executable and then under Proton, which required manually moving the save files from the Linux version so I didn't have to replay to this point. Apparently you are supposed to move diagonally by pressing two directions at the same time, or some crap like that, which is hard to do reliably without a keyboard. So no Steam Deck support! But even with a keyboard I couldn't do it. There is a reason why I religiously avoid action games.)

The offending puzzle is in the Ruins of Arei, which I guess is after about 40% of the total playtime (based on written walkthroughs, as I can't get past that point). Good job of totally destroying an absolutely fantastic first impression with a single unavoidable puzzle that doesn't fit in the game.

For those reading this who have no problem with action sequences: Up to that point it was a very lovely experience. Technically speaking, this game is nothing to write home about as it is basically an RPG Maker game. It's like a combination of the classical Earthbound/Mother RPGs (movement, general vibes) and the more story-heavy Jeff Vogel games (the Avadon series). In other words, it's extremely old fashioned. But it's quite polished except for some of the environment tiles being a bit hard to read: Sometimes it isn't clear how to get through a passage, e.g. because you are supposed to crawl when this possibility is not at all obvious from the graphics. But that would be a minor issue given that the story is very well done up to the point where I had to stop. (There are reports of a poor ending, but I can't comment on them.)

PS: It turns out that if you install the Windows edition of this game (on Linux this involves setting the compatibility tool to Proton rather than Linux runtime), the installation includes a file "Legacy.exe" with the original, Non-Broken Edition implemented in RPG Maker, which you can play instead of the broken 'Enhanced' Edition. In my case it was a bit more tricky because I need it to run in Steam so that Steam input can take care of my non-standard controller. ChatGPT talked me through this. (If there is interest I can explain how it works.) I am now very happily playing the Non-Broken Edition, which apparently has almost exactly the same content except for missing a variety of optional side quests as well as 'class quests' for the four main characters. On the positive side, there is the original normal puzzle that was replaced by the timed puzzle, and movement is much faster.

There is a major problem with the original edition, though. While combat in the 'Enhanced Edition' is motone and uninspired turn-based, the original edition has a weird hybrid system that may sound good in theory but is just stupid in practice. I recommend playing it in story mode so you don't get your characters killed while you are trying to figure out what's on the combat menu and how everything plays together. Here is how it actually works: If you just stare at the menu, the battle goes on without your input, with your characters only using very weak regular attacks, and doing so very slowly while quickly losing health points to more frequent enemy attacks. You can help by selecting a character and then selecting a special attack or other action for that character. This will then executed just once.

This game was amazing! As a big JRPG fan I didn't expect anything too crazy from this game since I had never really heard about it recommended and I saw it was initially made in RPG maker. However I was very very pleasantly surprised and will not stop singing this games praises!

 You can kind of tell that it was made with low resources but it does just about everything right and uses all of those resources perfectly. If anything it felt more impressive and inspiring that an RPG maker style game can actually be this good. It doesn't necessarily push the bounds of anything, but is clearly done with tons of care and executed very well. The characters and dialogue were so endearing and got me very quickly invested in the game, the exploration felt rewarding and enjoyable, the main story had me invested the whole time, and the combat holds up very well for typical turn based rpg standards. The game wasn't insanely long but was a solid length and felt just long enough to accomplish everything you want without getting to the point of it feeling repetitive or grindy. 

Only two very very minor issues I had. The first was the crawl function. This mechanic was perfectly fine but wasn't used super often and I would forget it existed and get stuck on points where I was suppose to crawl more than once. This is probably more my own issue than the game though lol. The other very small issue was that there was one very important boss fight that you are suppose to lose at the end. You can continuously use the reflect skill to stop this and make the fight endless. I didn't want to repeat the fight and had to look up if I should stop using reflect. You'll know the part where I am talking about and if you are questioning whether you are suppose to lose, yes you are. 

At the end of the day this game is absolutely amazing and you are certainly getting your moneys worth! I believe this studio has another game I will be buying next!
